body:
Hello, thank you for your contribution!

`CowData` is not, and cannot ever be, fully thread safe under writes. Even if this problem is fixed, there are many more potential ones that would only be fixable with something like `Mutex`. For example, it's always possible to simultaneously write and read a value from multiple threads, which can result in partial reads that yield random values. Other operations, like resizing, would create similar situations as fixed in this PR.

The correct fix for the problem at hand is, I think, to use a CoW copy of the vector across the two threads.

> The correct fix for the problem at hand is, I think, to use a CoW copy of the vector across the two threads.

Sorry, I should clarify. The code in question already does do this. The problem is with the `CowData` assignment operator.

Two threads are _not_ both writing to the underlying buffer at once. There's one writer. But currently _swapping_ a `CowData` out for another one briefly leaves readers without a `CowData` at all.

So it's essentially a double buffering issue.
Yes, I mean that you can have either infinite readers, or one writer (and no readers). One writer and one reader at the same time are not supported.

> One writer and one reader at the same time are not supported.

This seems like an unusual limitation for a game engine. I can see it currently doesn't work reliably, hence this PR. But is it really _intended_?

Populating buffers on a background thread swapping them and reading on the rendering thread is standard practice for games.

How else are existing APIs like `RenderingServerDefault`'s...

```cpp
	//these go through command queue if they are in another thread
	FUNC3(texture_2d_update, RID, const Ref<Image> &, int)
	FUNC2(texture_3d_update, RID, const Vector<Ref<Image>> &)
	FUNC4(texture_external_update, RID, int, int, uint64_t)
	FUNC2(texture_proxy_update, RID, RID)
```

.. supposed to be consumed?

They're documented as going through the command queue. That's why they're implemented via those macros. How would a background thread _ever_ safely update an `Image` using these APIs? You _cannot_ safely hang onto a `Mutex` in the presence of these command buffers. Our else you'll run into more deadlocks like this one I fixed over https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/110353

> Note that even with your fix, the change is not fully atomic. While it does significantly decrease the chance of crash, by removing the timeframe where _ptr is nullptr, there is still a chance of simultaneous read-write on _ptr. So, there's still chance of a crash.

I'm _definitely_ not going to pretend I'm 100% certain I've covered off everything. However, I can't see this. Are you able to elaborate?

The loop I've introduced in `_ref` is specifically designed to cover this. But it's certainly possible I've missed something.

Ah, right. You're talking about a torn read. Thanks for taking the time to put that together. Really appreciate it.

First, this isn't my area of expertise either, but I feel like a _lot_ of code would broken if I'm misunderstanding this topic... 😅 I don't think your example is necessarily an accurate test for trying to work out the cache line size for you architecture. Because you're writing in a loop, I don't think it's _guaranteed_ to give you the info you're after, unless the compiler optimizes away that loop because it's over a `constexpr` — I'd have to see what instructions compiler generates.

But yeah, a torn read could very well be an issue when a _single_ instruction writes across a cache boundary. Because whilst it's 1 instruction, the hardware needs to execute this operation in two steps. Then when you bring CPU caches into the mix, it's very possible that one thread on one core sees something different to a thread executing on another core.

_However_, most of the time torn reads aren't an issue because the C++ compiler will automatically align allocation so we're not straddling a cache line boundary. It'll insert padding as necessary to keep this alignment — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/cpp/alignment-cpp-declarations.

So in practice we won't observe torn reads of `p_from._ptr`. It's just a pointer, so it's a single instruction, and since it's aligned, it'll be atomic. Now, that doesn't mean that it's up-to-date by any stretch. That loop could very well see an old value, potentially even across multiple loops.

# `_ref`

As for how this impacts the the loop in `_ref`. Which by the way is critical to this PR. There's a screenshot / description of me observing this in practice, fixing the aforementioned Android camera bug, down the bottom of my original comment. So it is important. _But_ in writing this comment (discussion is good!) I've realized there is a flaw.

Whilst I'm never going to receive a garbage value of `p_from._ptr` i.e. it'll always be a real memory address. There's still nothing stop that value being freed _before_ my call to `_get_refcount((uint8_t *)from_ptr)->conditional_increment()`. If the memory isn't reallocated it'll all work out fine, there'll be a zero sitting there for the reference count and the increment will fail. But if the memory has been reallocated. Obtaining/incrementing the reference count will be a spectacular failure 🤦

Ugh, the only lock-free solution I can think of is to use something like [hazard pointers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazard_pointer). I'll try my hand at an implementation tomorrow. See if I can come up with something that doesn't add too much complexity.

That said, I really think there's a lot of value in trying to make this single writer, multiple readers approach work — particularly since I'd expect to be able to double buffer across threads by reassigning a `Vector` etc.

I'm not sure how cache lines play into the mix here (which may well be ignorance; I'm only somewhat familiar with such low level stuff). The most important property is, I believe, whether the CPU architecture guarantees atomicity from a single write instruction, and how large your write instruction is in assembly. On my computer, the code demonstrated that 16 bytes were atomic, which I think means that it has up to 16-byte atomic write instructions. I could probably have made it more reliable by aligning the byte array along its size, but it seems to have worked anyway.

But yes, overall, I'm referring to torn reads.

Anyway, before we get ahead of ourselves, I do have to stress again that `CowData` is not supposed to be multithread compatible. All you're getting is guarantees that multi-thread reads are safe, but as soon as writing is involved, you will be limited to one thread. If you need multi-thread access, it is expected you create copies, or use mutexes.

If there's a consensus at the core meeting to go with it, we'll increase `CowData`'s robustness to cross-thread assignments, as you described, by making it somewhat atomic. But in any case, it will continue to be an officially unsupported scenario, especially if anything except `_ptr` assignment is involved.

Realistically I don't think there's any way to make this happen without _some_ observable performance impact _for the assignment operator_. I think that's reasonable. However, if every _access_ of ptr itself is slower, I agree, that's not acceptable.

I must admit I'm also not certain what impact the introduction of `volatile` would have for general access. I'd _expect_ it to be imperceptible since it effectively just disables optimizations that I wouldn't expect to be coming into play. _But_ admittedly, that's just an assumption. It's the kind of thing that would warrant some tests to validate, for sure.

The ABI change means this particular solution is a no go anyway. I liked the simplicity of the reader count living on `CowData`, at face value anyway 😅 But yeah, not happening.

I _think_ I'd need to use hazard pointers after all. But I'm not going to lie, they're kind of yuck. There are plenty of advantages on a technical level e.g. memory use scales with the number of threads, not the number of `CowData`. There's no denying it's more complexity though.

However, the reality is that whilst not having `CowData` provide this guarantee, its implementation is simpler, it's just pushing the complexity onto consumers. Since there are many consumers, both in the engine, and user code, that means lots more complexity overall. For example, the Android camera server problem — the solution without this `CowData` guarantee is _exceedingly_ complex due to the interplay of the command queue and mutexes.

I still need to prove that the introduction of `volatile` doesn't cause any performance degradation. However, I'm reasonably happy with the implementation I just pushed.

There's no need for the crazy complexity of a full blown hazard pointer implementation. This is fairly simple self contained solution. It's significantly more performant than hazard pointers, since the writer only has to check one variable (not one per thread). Better still, the memory cost is fixed up front, irrespective of both the number of threads and `CowData`. The trade-off is that we have shared reader count "buckets", which means _in theory_ in _extraordinarily_ unlikely situations our unref spinlock could spin a little more than is strictly necessary.

Of course, I understand the core team have to decide they're actually interested in improving `CowData`'s assignment thread safety in general. If I can propose what the fix could look like in practice, then hopefully that's able to make any conversations that do take place a little less hypothetical.
@Ivorforce I've just converted this to a draft because it's definitely not in a mergeable state, irrespective of whether it's actually decided this is wanted.
